title: Replying to @thelandonhudson #broadway #musicaltheatre #kristinchenow...
transcript: I really didn't think I'd be defending the Queen of Versailles, and in many ways, I still won't. This new musical, with what seems to be a dream team on paper, including Kristin Chenoweth, Steven Schwartz and Michael Arden, has been pretty swiftly rejected by the Broadway community. And after all that word of mouth, it wasn't quite the disaster I was expecting it to be. But I can't say that I liked it there. To me, its biggest crime, on an artistic level at least, was just being extremely bland. But I frankly could say that about a lot of Broadway musicals these days. But the other big criticism that's been looming over this musical is that its subject, Jackie Seigel, is not only a supporter of our current president, but perhaps not the best person in other ways as well. And I went into the show with that at the forefront of my mind. So imagine my surprise to find that the show does not paint her in a positive light. Like, it's actually quite critical of her. And I went in not knowing much about her, and I left thinking, wow, he's really not a good person. There are times when she's written more sympathetically, but it's in the moments where she's being tempted to turn to her more human, grounded roots. She's someone who's lost her sense of humanity to this lifestyle of vapid excess. And in that sense, she is a tragic figure. Like I Wasn't rooting for her to get what she wants, but I was rooting for her to want something else. But at virtually every turn the musical makes it pretty clear that she fails to meaningfully do so. But wait, you might be asking, isn't the real Jackie Seagal directly involved with this musical? Like, how can they be against her if she approves of it? Well, even in the show itself they make it pretty clear that she cares way more about having the spotlight than she does about whether it's positive or negative. So her approving of a show that's critical of her is not so confusing or far fetched. But then you might say, well, why play into it? Why give her the attention that she's after? And I do understand that logic, but I don't totally agree with it. Because if the goal is to use her as a warning against the dangers of excess wealth, then ideally. Maybe less so in practice, which I'll talk about in a second. But in theory, there's more benefit in conveying that to tens of thousands of audience members than there is in just trying to fight her specifically however you can. Having said all of that, I do still think there are ways in which the critique falls short. There are moments that sometimes stray too far into that territory of like what a hard working optimist she is, and that can sometimes make the aim of the show Feel not confused exactly, but diluted. I don't doubt that the show is ultimately critical of her, but that criticism isn't as sharp or as impactful as it could have been. there's room for nuance. Not everything has to be a black and white message. But it didn't feel nuanced as much as it felt unfocused. And frankly, some of that might be a result of Kristin Chenoweth's performance, where she seems to be trying to play the character as warm and likable as possible, even when the writing doesn't necessarily reflect that. And like, I've heard that the show actually works much better with Sherry Renee Scott in the role because of her somewhat colder, harder demeanor, and I completely believe it. But ultimately, no, I didn't particularly enjoy it as a piece of theater. Still, I don't object to its mere existence the way I think a lot of people do.
